name: Bacopa monnieri

card.summary: Ayurvedic "brahmi" herb sold as a memory nootropic; trials are small and reviews call the evidence for cognition inconclusive.
card.note: FDA has sent warning letters over unproven disease claims on Bacopa products; not approved as a drug.

quick.overview:
Bacopa monnieri is a creeping wetland herb used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine, where it is called brahmi and associated with memory and learning. Today extracts are sold as dietary supplements and discussed as a nootropic.

Small human trials have looked at memory and cognition in healthy adults and older people, but Wikipedia reports no good evidence that it improves cognitive performance, and the research literature describes results that vary with extract type. It has no documented role in appearance treatment.
quick.mechanism: Its main constituents are bacosides, triterpenoid saponins. Laboratory and animal work reports antioxidant activity and effects on cholinergic and other neurotransmitter systems, but how this relates to human cognition is not established.
quick.risks: The most commonly reported effects are nausea, increased bowel motility and stomach upset. In 2019 the US FDA sent warning letters to supplement makers over unproven claims (Alzheimer's, anxiety, blood pressure and others) and stated that no Bacopa product is approved for medical use.

lead: Bacopa monnieri, known as brahmi or water hyssop, is a creeping perennial herb of tropical and subtropical wetlands that is used in Ayurvedic medicine, where it has traditionally been associated with memory and learning.[1][2] Its best-characterised constituents are the bacosides, a family of dammarane-type triterpenoid saponins.[1]

In supplement markets it is sold as a "nootropic". Reviews describe preclinical work on antioxidant and neuropharmacological effects[3][4], while Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence that it improves cognitive performance and memory.[1] Grokipedia (an AI-generated encyclopedia) describes randomized trials as suggesting possible cognitive benefits with results varying by extract and dose.[5]

Bacopa is not an appearance intervention; its presence in looksmaxxing-adjacent "recovery" and nootropic discussions reflects general interest in cognition and stress. In the United States it is not an approved drug, and the FDA issued warning letters in 2019 about unproven health claims.[1]
infobox: Dietary supplement; no approved medical use

paras: In Ayurveda the plant has been used as a memory-enhancing, sedative and anti-inflammatory herb.[3] Supplement marketing today emphasises memory, focus and stress.[5]

Wikipedia lists the bacosides (about twelve analogs) and related bacopasides as the main characterised compounds, along with alkaloids and other plant chemicals.[1] Rodent studies have reported antioxidant activity in brain regions such as the frontal cortex, striatum and hippocampus[6], and anticholinesterase and cognition-related effects in comparison with Ginkgo biloba extracts.[7] A rodent model study reported neuroprotective effects in an Alzheimer's disease model.[8] These findings are preclinical.

A 2001 placebo-controlled study in Psychopharmacology examined the chronic effects of a Bacopa extract on cognitive function in healthy human subjects.[9] Reviews of the nootropic literature have described the human evidence as limited by small trials and differing extracts.[3][4] Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence that it improves cognitive performance.[1]

Registered trials listed on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies of working memory in students[11], BDNF levels and memory[12], cognition and anxiety with pharmacokinetics[13], children's cognition with a micronutrient beverage[14], and vascular oxidative stress[15], as well as a Phase 2 study in Gulf War illness[16] and an earlier Phase 2 trial in schizophrenia.[17] Registry entries show design and status, not results.

The most commonly reported effects in humans are nausea, increased intestinal motility and gastrointestinal upset.[1] Grokipedia also lists dry mouth, headache, fatigue and drowsiness as less common.[5]

In 2019 the FDA sent warning letters to supplement manufacturers whose claims concerned conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, anxiety and high blood pressure, which the agency described as unproven, and stated that no B. monnieri products are approved for medical purposes.[1]

timeline.event: FDA warning letters to supplement manufacturers over unproven Bacopa health claims.[1]
